I have used and continue to use this license, as it satisfies my needs exactly w/r/t how I prefer my code be used. I see that although it isn't incredibly widely used that 76 separate public github repos use it currently, which means that many people have gone to the trouble of finding an unlisted license that satisfies their licensing needs, as I have. Most of my repos are private, so I can also conclude that 76 is a conservative estimate of the number of repos where this license is used. There are also many examples of this license being used off github, as @caass shared above.

As with any license, integration into SPDX will make it more widely available and increase use considerably. I personally would find it very helpful if it was listed in SPDX. discussed on 5/25/2023 call: Steve did a compare to CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0 - key changes in section 4(b) on what kinds of commercial activity is allowed. Is this "more permissive" than the NC restrictions in CC-BY-NC?

@swinslow to do write-up and then people can comment on that

The main difference b/w this and `CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0` is that an exception is added to the non-commercial restriction in `CC-BY-NA-3.0`

As a reminder, the non-commercial restriction in `CC-BY-NA-3.0` states:  "You may not exercise any of the rights granted to You in Section 3 above in any manner that is primarily intended for or directed to ward commercial advantage or private monetary compensation."

This license adds: 
"c. You may exercise the rights granted in Section 3 for commercial purposes only if:
    i. You are a Worker-owned business or Worker-owned collective; and
    ii. All financial gain, surplus, profits and benefits produced by the business or collective are distributed among the Workerowners
d. Any use by a business that is privately owned and managed, and that seeks to generate profit from the labor of employees paid by salary or other wages, is not permitted under this license."

Regardless of whether this could be deemed more or less restrictive than what `CC-BY-NA-3.0` already states, the additional language seems like it contradicts itself, is undefined, and would be very difficult to enforce.
- "Worker-owned" is not defined
- it states that "All financial gain, surplus, profits and benefits produced by the business or collective are distributed among the Workerowners" but then says that use by a business that "seeks to generate profit from the labor of employees paid by salary or other wages" is not permitted. But those profits be distributed to the worker owners as per the previous part?? This seems a bit circular
- most business financial records are going to be confidential (unless it's a non-profit or some other designation that requires public disclosure) so how would one know if this requirement is met?
- questionable enforceability if the condition falls outside the nexus of copyright rights as an unilateral license

Note - these are just things off the top of head, not intended to be a full legal analysis.

But given the issues with the drafting, I have a hard time thinking that this license is going to rise to substantial use in the software supply chain such that there is a need to have it represented in an SBOM?

Hey all, just fyi, the ppl was written in co-operation with John Magyar, 
who is a lawyer with a PhD in statutory interpretation.

The contradiction is intentional, as the restriction is lifted when the 
conditions are met, and worker owned is defined as "All financial gain, 
surplus, profits and benefits produced by the business or collective are 
distributed among the Workerowners"

John is CCed.

Best

Regarding @jlovejoy's final comment, notability certainly comes into play, but I'd wager that visibility and representation contribute greatly to license use. Creative Commons licenses, for example, have enjoyed massive success not just because Lawrence Lessing is well known for Eldred v Ashcroft, but because the Creative Commons nonprofit itself affords them much greater visibility overall than licenses without such a high profile organization backing them up.

Seconding @morien's remarks here -- aside from the issue of "the license is unpopular, so there is no need to represent it in an SBOM", are there any other concerns still blocking this? Is that concern alone enough to prohibit the license from SPDX?

First off, the formal review for this one has been lingering for far, far too long, and that's my fault. I want to apologize sincerely to the license submitters for waiting so long for a response here; that's on me and I appreciate your patience.

Having reviewed it in line with the [SPDX License Inclusion Principles](https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/blob/main/DOCS/license-inclusion-principles.md), I'm in favor of adding this one to the License List.
